big_case_rationale: Transsubstantive FRCP question that matters to everyday civil litigation practice, but a technical pleading-procedure ruling with low public salience.

semantic_claims.proposition: The majority rests on the text of the interlocking pleading-and-amendment rules: Rule 8(c)(1)'s command that a party 'must affirmatively state any avoidance or affirmative defense,' read with Rule 15(a)(2) and Rule 16(b)(4) as the exclusive routes for adding an omitted defense after the scheduling-order deadline, means a defendant may not assert a never-pleaded affirmative defense for the first time in a summary-judgment motion without amending (or obtaining constructive amendment of) its answer; the Eleventh Circuit's Hassan no-prejudice gloss is rejected as an atextual, purpose-based standard that lets motion practice circumvent the amendment rules, and the respondent's Rule 61 harmless-error and 'purely legal argument' theories are rejected as overriding the Rules' plain terms.

The majority states a categorical, transsubstantive rule for all federal civil litigation — an unpleaded affirmative defense may be raised at summary judgment only via proper amendment under Rules 15 and 16 (or party consent under Rule 15(b)) — rather than a holding confined to this case's scheduling-order posture or to the Title VII personal-staff exemption; it does not decide whether Younge was in fact 'personal staff,' remanding for further proceedings under the correct standard.
